attachments.insertion_landmark: 1st metatarsal base, medial cuneiform (via a long plantar course)

actions: everts the ankle, assists plantarflexion, supports the transverse (metatarsal) arch

functional_compartments.name: Single fiber population
functional_compartments.function_note: Its tendon crosses the entire plantar surface of the foot from lateral to medial (via the cuboid tunnel), the longest tendon course of any lower-limb muscle relative to its origin.
functional_compartments.source: Ward SR, Eng CM, Smallwood LH, Lieber RL (2009) Clin Orthop Relat Res 467:1074-1082 -- lower-extremity muscle architecture (fascicle length, PCSA, sarcomere length) cadaver dataset

motor_endplate_zones.method: cadaveric dissection of the superficial fibular nerve's motor entry point (MEP)
motor_endplate_zones.notes: Mean reference line length 33.4 +/- 2.5 cm across 43 cadaveric legs. The nerve branch to fibularis longus itself leaves the superficial fibular nerve trunk at approximately 10% along this line, then enters the muscle within the 20-40% band reported here.
motor_endplate_zones.source: Lee JH, Lee BN, An X, Chung RH, Kwon SO, Han SH (2011), Clinical Anatomy 24(2):232-236, doi:10.1002/ca.21076 (https://doi.org/10.1002/ca.21076) -- retrieved via PubMed

source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998); Ward SR, Eng CM, Smallwood LH, Lieber RL (2009) Clin Orthop Relat Res 467:1074-1082 -- lower-extremity muscle architecture (fascicle length, PCSA, sarcomere length) cadaver dataset

trigger_points.location_description: Muscle belly over the proximal-to-middle third of the fibula, on the lateral aspect of the leg.
trigger_points.referred_pain_pattern: Pain projecting around the lateral malleolus (above, behind and below it) and into the lateral aspect of the foot, with a band of pain also felt over the middle third of the lateral leg; associated paresthesia/numbness can extend into the third, fourth and great toes.
trigger_points.activation_perpetuating_factors: Ankle sprain (especially inversion injury), prolonged immobilization (cast, plantarflexed sleeping posture), leg crossing, flat feet, and high heels -- all of which chronically load or compress the peroneal muscles.
trigger_points.notes: Distinct from but often confused with lateral ankle ligament sprain or peroneal tendinopathy; usually discussed together with fibularis brevis given overlapping referral zones.
trigger_points.source: Simons, Travell & Simons Trigger Point Manual, Vol. 2 (Lower Extremities), 1999 -- as cited in secondary summaries (e.g. Morningside Acupuncture NYC 'Peroneus Longus Trigger Points', muscle-joint-pain.com peroneus longus/brevis/tertius reference) describing the lateral-leg trigger point site and lateral-malleolus/foot referral pattern with toe paresthesia
